cards.title: Surprise, read as malfunction
cards.body: Four pieces today press on the same nerve: what a system gives up when you engineer the surprise out of it. A Fed chair argues markets should have to read the economy instead of his intentions; a case for paidia says scorekeeping ate the kind of play that has no point; and Dostoevsky's narrator, on Day 3, would sooner insist twice two makes five than live somewhere everything has already been calculated for him. The one not to miss is the first Air Force pilot to fly with an autonomous wingman, trained since day one to treat any surprise from a machine as a malfunction and now having to sort out which surprises are the aircraft being right.

cards.title: DMT slides brain waves toward static, and the self goes with them
cards.body: The brain normally runs just shy of chaos, in a state physicists call criticality, where past electrical activity keeps echoing into future activity. A new study found DMT knocks it off that edge — and the further a person's alpha and theta waves slid away from criticality, the more completely they reported their sense of self coming apart.
cards.evidence: two pooled samples · n=27 · within-subject saline placebo · EEG + self-report

sections.text:
Twenty-seven healthy adults lay under EEG caps while DMT went into a vein. On a different day, the same people got saline. After the drug wore off, they were handed a questionnaire, and the researchers cared most about one line on it: whether they had experienced "a disintegration of my usual sense of 'self' or 'ego.'"

That dissolution turns out to have a physical signature, and the signature is a loss of structure.

The physics term is criticality: the exact boundary between rigid order and total chaos, where the healthy human brain normally sits. Being near that boundary is what lets regions talk to each other efficiently across both short and long distances, and it produces the rich variety of wave patterns that ordinary conscious awareness seems to require.

It also gives the brain long-range temporal correlations. The echoes linger instead of fading out quickly — a short-term biological memory that holds a stream of thought together and keeps a sense of identity stable across minutes.

To measure how close a brain sits to that edge, the team used detrended fluctuation analysis, which spits out a single number. Near one means highly structured and complex, what engineers call pink noise. Near one half means random and structureless, the static of white noise.

Under DMT, those numbers dropped across theta waves (memory), alpha waves (relaxed wakefulness), and beta waves (active thinking). The signals slid toward static.

Then the team asked which way the brain had fallen off the edge, using a newly developed metric for the ratio of excitatory to inhibitory activity. You might expect a psychedelic to overheat the system into a supercritical, overactive state. Alpha and beta went the other direction: subcritical, dominated by inhibitory signals. High randomness, low complexity. Not a brain firing wilder patterns, but a brain whose patterns lost their intricate architecture.

And the two halves lined up. The size of that slide, in alpha and theta, tracked how completely people said their self had come apart.

This sharpens the entropic brain hypothesis, the popular claim that psychedelics increase the brain's randomness. The randomness is real — but it arrives with a drop in statistical complexity, not a rise. In some scientific framings the two move together; here they split. The signal becomes less predictable and less richly varied at the same time.

What makes the result strange is the company it keeps. The researchers note that this shift away from criticality resembles what shows up under general anesthesia and in deep meditation — states that feel nothing like a DMT trip and nothing like each other. What they share is the breakdown of the normal, self-reflective stream of thought. A subcritical alpha shift may be the common marker: not a measure of what you're experiencing, but of whether there's still a someone doing the experiencing.

sections.label: The experiment
sections.text: The team pooled two studies, 27 healthy adults total. Each person received intravenous DMT on one day and a saline placebo on another. EEG ran from before the injection through twenty minutes after, and participants rated their subjective experience once the effects had worn off. Lead authors Mona Irrmischer and Marco Aqil, in The Journal of Neuroscience.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: Twenty-seven people, and the link between criticality and ego dissolution is a correlation between a brain measure and a retrospective self-rating. The bigger limit is the instrument: scalp EEG mostly captures slower waves. Faster oscillations, harder to detect from outside the skull, might be doing the opposite — going supercritical — and the authors suggest that's where the vivid imagery and emotional content of the trip could live.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The self isn't a thing the brain contains. It's a structure the brain keeps rebuilding out of its own echoes — and the echoes can go quiet.

recall.q: DMT made brain activity more random. Why is reading that as "more complex" the wrong lesson from this study?
recall.a: Because here randomness and complexity moved in opposite directions. Detrended fluctuation analysis values slid from pink noise toward white — the waves lost their long-range temporal structure — and the excitation-to-inhibition metric put alpha and beta on the subcritical, inhibition-dominated side. Less predictable and less richly varied at once, not a richer brain.

cards.title: Day 3 · Twice two makes five
cards.body: The case against the Palace of Crystal reaches its peak today — and then the arguer takes the whole thing back. What survives the retraction is the thing this book has been circling all along: a memory, and the wet snow.

sections.text:
Free will trained to coincide with arithmetic is not free will. Twice two makes four whether you consent or not — so what, he asks, is left to want?

Then he backs off: he is joking, his jokes aren't brilliant, he is "jesting against the grain." The retreat is tactical. From it he flips the burden of proof — you want to reform man's will by science, but how do you know his inclinations need reforming, or that it would benefit him? "It may be the law of logic, but not the law of humanity."

Then he grants their premise so completely it breaks in his hands. Man is a creative animal, an engineer, made "incessantly and eternally to make new roads, wherever they may lead." So why does he love destruction and chaos too? Because "he is instinctively afraid of attaining his object and completing the edifice he is constructing." He loves the building from a distance, wants to build it rather than live in it, and leaves it when finished to les animaux domestiques — the ants, the sheep, whose ant-heap endures forever. Man is a chess player who loves the game, not the end of it.

That is the day's real thesis, and it isn't a joke: perhaps the only goal is the process of attaining, "in life itself, and not in the thing to be attained." Anything attained hardens into a formula, "and such positiveness is not life, gentlemen, but is the beginning of death." So man crosses oceans hunting mathematical certainty and dreads finding it, because "when he has found it there will be nothing for him to look for." Workmen at least finish, get paid, go to the tavern, get taken to the police-station — occupation for a week. "But where can man go?"

Patience gone, the argument turns to abuse: twice two makes four is "a pert coxcomb who stands with arms akimbo barring your path and spitting." And he offers his counter-currency, twice two makes five.

Then the turn that undoes his own opening. Perhaps man loves suffering as much as well-being — don't consult history, "only ask yourself, if you are a man and have lived at all." He takes neither side: he holds no brief for suffering or well-being, only "for my caprice, and for its being guaranteed to me when necessary." Suffering is unthinkable in the crystal palace because suffering means doubt. And then, quietly: "suffering is the sole origin of consciousness." The disease he began by cursing is the one thing he would never trade.

Chapter X names what he is actually refusing. He'd crawl into a hen-house to stay dry but won't call it a palace out of gratitude. The palace's crime is that it can never be destroyed and you cannot put your tongue out at it, even on the sly — and he insists it isn't that he enjoys the gesture. What he resents is that nobody has built the thing he wouldn't want to mock. "Destroy my desires, eradicate my ideals, show me something better, and I will follow you." Until then, not one brick.

Then he detonates the structure himself. "Hurrah for underground!" — and instantly, "even now I am lying!" It isn't underground he wants but "something different, quite different, for which I am thirsting, but which I cannot find." He believes not one word he has written; he is "lying like a cobbler." He then writes out his readers' contempt for him — you have no respect for your own suffering, you hide your last word from fear — and admits he invented that too, after forty years listening through a crack under the floor.

What survives, once the argument is confessed as bluff, is memory. He wants to test whether a man can be open even with himself. Heine says true autobiography is impossible and Rousseau lied from vanity; he agrees, and starts anyway. One memory haunts him "like an annoying tune that one cannot get rid of." Snow is falling, yellow and dingy.

Part II. He is twenty-four, in the office, unable to hold anyone's gaze. The mechanism is exact: out of "unbounded vanity" and an impossible standard he looks at himself with loathing — hating his face, willing to look base if only he could look intelligent — and then reads that loathing on every face around him.

sections.label: From the book
sections.text: Every man has reminiscences which he would not tell to everyone, but only to his friends. He has other matters in his mind which he would not reveal even to his friends, but only to himself, and that in secret. But there are other things which a man is afraid to tell even to himself, and every decent man has a number of such things stored away in his mind. The more decent he is, the greater the number of such things in his mind.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: He loves the process of attaining, but does not quite like to have attained.

recall.q: Why does he think man loves destruction and chaos as much as he loves building?
recall.a: Because man is afraid of finishing. He loves the edifice from a distance and doesn't want to live in it — the goal is "the incessant process of attaining," life itself, since anything attained hardens into a formula as positive as twice two, and "such positiveness is not life... but is the beginning of death."
