cards.title: How Amazon's mega dropdown avoids the hover delay
cards.body: Amazon's Shop by Department menu has no hover delay and no diagonal-reach bug — a combination most nested menus can't manage. It isn't tracking which row your cursor is on. It's tracking where the cursor is headed.

sections.text:
You move diagonally toward an open submenu. Halfway across, your path clips the row below, the submenu swaps for a different one, and the thing you were reaching for is gone.

The usual fix is a timer: wait a couple hundred milliseconds before honoring a new row's hover, and the diagonal path survives. The cost is that every deliberate move down the list now feels sluggish — the author points at an old Khan Academy menu where you can watch the delay happen. Skip the timer and you get the other failure instead: Bootstrap's dropdowns switch immediately and turn the submenu into a target you can't hit.

Amazon's trick: at any moment, draw a triangle from the current cursor position to the upper-right and lower-right corners of the open dropdown. That triangle is the cone of paths that lead into the submenu. If your next mouse position lands inside it, you're aiming at the submenu, so the submenu stays put — it doesn't matter that you passed over "Appstore for Android" on the way to "Learn more about Cloud Drive." If the next position falls outside, you've changed your mind, and the menu switches with no delay at all. The responsiveness and the forgiveness come from the same test.

The author packaged it as a jQuery plugin, jQuery-menu-aim, and shipped it in Khan Academy's Learn menu. Amazon detects containment in the triangle with a cross product; he admits he used a cruder slope comparison because he'd lost his intuition for the linear algebra. Both work. The insight, not the math, is the expensive part — and he suspects this one has been solved, forgotten, and rediscovered many times already.

sections.label: Do this
items: Before reaching for a hover timeout, ask whether the cursor's last position already answers the question — keep it, and compare it against the triangle formed by the cursor and the two far corners of the open panel.
Make leaving the triangle the trigger, not entering a new row: while the path aims into the submenu, ignore row hovers entirely; the instant it stops aiming, switch with zero delay.
Skip the cross product if the vectors don't come naturally — two slope comparisons give you the same containment test in a few lines.
Audit every nested menu, tooltip, and popover in your app the same way: move the cursor diagonally toward it at speed and see whether it survives the trip.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: A timeout is a guess about intent. Amazon measured the intent instead.

recall.q: Amazon's mega dropdown switches submenus instantly and still lets you reach diagonally. What is it testing, instead of which row the cursor is currently over?
recall.a: Where the cursor is headed. It draws a triangle from the current mouse position to the two far corners of the open submenu; if the next position lands inside that triangle you're aiming at the submenu, so it stays open regardless of which rows you cross — and the moment you leave the triangle, it switches with no delay.

cards.title: Household logistics is unpaid work with a military history
cards.body: Mrs Beeton's 1861 household manual has barely needed revision. The tools changed — handmade bread and clothes, then the washing machine, then delivery apps — and the work stayed exactly where it was. Susan Zieger traces the woman it addresses back to Napoleon's supply columns, where the word logistics was coined, and forward through the Gilbreths' time-and-motion children to Ghislaine Maxwell. Every version does the same job: organising and supplying for the man who holds the money and makes the decisions.

sections.text:
Before a charge, someone moved down the line handing out shots of brandy. When it was over, someone dragged the wounded back out of range. Often that someone was a soldier's wife, walking behind the column with the tobacco, the clean clothes and the alcohol.

The word logistics entered the language in the 19th century to explain how Napoleon had taken Europe: the science of supplying soldiers and moving them into strategic position. The Napoleonic Code entitled a soldier to bring his wife, on the understanding that she was his legal property, obliged to follow wherever he went. The theorist Paul Virilio gave her a name — the logistical spouse.

Susan Zieger's essay is a history of that figure after the wars ended. She never disappears. She changes settings.

By 1861 she has a manual. Mrs Beeton's Book of Household Management, a bestseller and a reference work for generations, opens by stating the comparison outright: "As with the commander of an army, or the leader of any enterprise, so is it with the mistress of a house." Isabella Beeton's programme was early rising, cleanliness, frugality, and the canny management of accounts and family entertainment — the middle-class wife spending her husband's income to keep the operation stocked and in order.

What strikes Zieger is how little of that advice ever needed revision. It survived the shift from handmaking food and clothes to operating a washing machine, then the shift to ordering everything through apps. Women gained civil rights, incomes and independence across two centuries; men moved from taking actual territory to opening sales territory. The logistical work stayed exactly where it was.

Then comes the essay's strangest exhibit. Frank Gilbreth, an industrial engineer, and his wife Lillian, an engineer and psychologist, invented the flow chart, ran motion studies that broke factory tasks into their smallest movements to find the most efficient sequence, and had twelve children — the family behind Cheaper by the Dozen. Their rule for the shop floor: "an unnecessary motion is money lost forever."

They ran the house as an annex of the laboratory. The children bathed fast, soaping their limbs in a regimented order, while German and French lessons played from Victrola phonographs installed in the bathrooms; before bed they initialled charts certifying that homework was done, teeth brushed, faces washed. The children, Zieger notes, come out looking uncannily like anonymous workers or mass-produced items — which is the point. Domestic logistics doesn't only supply and coordinate a household. It manufactures and trains efficient workers for the order that will employ them.

The current iteration is the tradwife making her own bread and cleaning fluids, and the most-watched version fuses it with Christian patriarchy. On 19 Kids and Counting, Michelle and Jim Bob Duggar, devout Baptists who shunned birth control, managed an enormous brood as a divine operations problem. Michelle wrote the foreword to Kim Brenneman's Large Family Logistics (2010), which supplied the systems: timed chores, pairing each child with a buddy, giving every child extra attention on the same fixed day each week. Trust God, and the details work themselves out.

The show ended in scandal. The Duggars' eldest son had molested several of his sisters and a babysitter; he was later convicted and sentenced for possessing child pornography, and more recently a brother was arrested on charges of sexually abusing a nine-year-old girl. Zieger refuses to file this as an unrelated failure — such crimes, she argues, are a feature of patriarchal, misogynist households rather than a bug. All the feeding, clothing, organising, educating and indoctrinating did not make the children safe from each other. And modelling that subservience for the girls trains them into the same unpaid logistics later, including the supply of sex within marriage, which is where the Napoleonic Code came in.

The darkest case needs no household at all. Ghislaine Maxwell was the logistician of Jeffrey Epstein's trafficking operation, which involved more than a thousand victims; she confiscated many of their passports and booked them onto the private jet to the island. As girlfriend and pimp she supplied sex directly and by proxy, and Zieger points at the etymology joining the roles: procurement is the branch of logistics that handles sourcing, and a procurer arranges sex work. The labour had commercial value beyond the abuse — data from the enterprise likely fed blackmail, new connections and closed deals.

Across battlefield, drawing room and jet: he makes the money, she spends it. He decides, she coordinates.

Zieger dates the arrangement to the 17th century and the rise of European capitalism, when states barred women from independently accessing their own wages and pushed them toward producing more workers instead. Women kept working; the work simply stopped being paid, and dependence followed, costing them further rights. Alongside transatlantic slavery, that free labour propped up a faltering system — and as Silvia Federici has argued, this unvalued work still amounts to most of the work done on the planet.

So how does the burden move? The late-2010s answer was the emotional labour conversation, which was really about logistics: the overwhelm came from holding every household detail in mind and always being the one to initiate. LGBTQ+ households divided the load more evenly, if not at parity. Heterosexual men, in Zieger's blunt reading, seemed unable to receive the message — as one divorced man put it in a viral 2016 essay, his wife had wanted him to apply the same intelligence and learning capacity he used everywhere else to the logistics of running their lives.

Couples tried chore charts, transferring duties from her column to his. Then the pandemic hit and home schooling landed on women, who traded careers and mental health to keep households running. Where her salary was the smaller one, her stepping back was the economically rational move — which is precisely how a pay gap compounds itself. Intransigence, economic inequity and conservative traditionalism all retrenched; some women gave up and turned to tradwife content, others appear to be avoiding men altogether.

Zieger's own answer is deliberately unglamorous, and far smaller than the history preceding it. Not trends and life hacks but the long view: recognising that what looks like a relationship problem has a name, a history, and a scale running from the household up to the state. Once she started calling her daily coordination logistics, she could see the same labour operating in her community and her country — and could treat a lifetime of unpaid practice as accumulated skill she gets to decide where to aim.

sections.label: Steelman
sections.text: The pattern is assembled from cases selected because they fit it, and the range strains: a Victorian cookbook, a reality TV family and a convicted sex trafficker are doing very different things, and Maxwell in particular is a criminal outlier asked to illuminate ordinary marriages. The closing move is vulnerable too — recognising your own organisational skill and choosing where to direct it is a private reframe, not far from the individual life hacks the essay dismisses a paragraph earlier.

sections.label: Key takeaways
items: The Napoleonic Code entitled a soldier to bring his wife on campaign as his legal property, obliged to follow him anywhere; Virilio named her the logistical spouse.

The Gilbreth children took French and German lessons from bathroom phonographs and initialled nightly charts certifying teeth brushed and homework done. Zieger's read: household logistics doesn't only run a home, it manufactures trained workers for the order that will employ them.

The unpaid arrangement is a 17th-century policy outcome, not a natural one: states blocked women from independently accessing their wages and steered them toward producing more workers. The work continued; the pay stopped, and dependence followed.
COVID reversed the chore-splitting trend by pure arithmetic — when hers is the smaller salary, her stepping back is the rational household choice and the compounding move for a pay gap.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: "An unnecessary motion is money lost forever," the Gilbreths told the shop floor. Upstairs, in the same house, the motions were never money to begin with.

recall.q: Zieger tracks one figure from Napoleon's supply columns to the tradwife. What is she called, and what does the essay argue her labour produces beyond a running household?
recall.a: Virilio's logistical spouse: she organises, supplies and coordinates for the man who holds the capital, the status and the decisions. On the Gilbreth evidence, the work also manufactures and trains the next generation of efficient workers — children bathed in regimented order, initialling nightly compliance charts.

cards.title: 1967 — on this day
cards.body: Paddy Roy Bates proclaimed HM Fort Roughs, a former World War II Maunsell Sea Fort in the North Sea off the coast of Suffolk, England, as an independent sovereign state: the Principality of Sealand (pictured).

cards.title: Didion on why we must let the dead stay dead
cards.body: Joan Didion ends The Year of Magical Thinking by arguing for release on geological grounds rather than emotional ones: hills slump, waterfalls correct themselves, islands are temporary features. She knows exactly why we keep the dead alive — to keep them with us — and says that past a point we pay the upkeep out of our own living.

sections.text:
One morning, well into her widowhood, Joan Didion woke and tried to recall the arrangement of the rooms in a house she had left decades earlier — the place in Brentwood Park where she and John Gregory Dunne had been young together. She walked it in her mind, the ground floor first, then upstairs. Later that day she realized she had forgotten one of the rooms.

The lapse sits near the end of The Year of Magical Thinking, her reckoning with the death of Dunne, her husband of four decades. Those closing pages work as a field guide for letting go of anything at all.

The setup is the old contract: to love something is to make yourself available to losing it, and we sign anyway. Judith Viorst's version is that nobody becomes a separate, responsible, connected, reflective person without some measure of losing and leaving. What we keep of our losses builds the person we become; what we let die inside us — the tortured patterns, the ill-serving habits, the beliefs that fence us in — is what makes another life possible.

The difficulty is that letting go cannot be decided on. It can only be surrendered to, and the surrender arrives with denial, dissociation, and the thousand small lies we tell in order to keep holding.

Didion's way into it isn't emotional. It's geological.

She was a geologist's grandchild, and learned early to expect hills, waterfalls, even islands to be mutable. When a hill slumps into the ocean she sees the order in it. When a 5.2 on the Richter scale wrenches the writing table in her own room in her own house, she keeps typing. A hill, in that vocabulary, is a temporary accommodation to stress. A waterfall is a stream correcting its own misfit with the rock beneath. Oahu — a young landmass along the Hawaiian Ridge, already eroding — is a temporary feature whose tenure as the Crossroads of the Pacific gets shorter with every rainfall and every tremor along the Pacific plates. Transience isn't a defect in things. It's what things are.

Then the ritual. When she carried Dunne's ashes to St. John the Divine, she brought a lei — the South Pacific garland you hang on someone arriving or departing. She had lived and written in Hawaii, and she remembered the custom from the years when people still left Honolulu on the Matson Lines: at the moment of departure you threw your lei into the water, and the throw was a promise that the traveler would return.

The leis got caught in the ship's wake and went bruised and brown — the same two words she uses for the gardenias that collected in the pool filter at the Brentwood Park house. A promise of return, performed with an object everyone can see rotting. She doesn't press the point. She just notes that the lei she left at the cathedral would have gone brown by now.

Leis brown, plates shift, islands vanish, rooms get forgotten. The move is to make the small deaths count as practice — the failed projects, the ended relationships, the plans that quietly expired are a scale model of the hardest losses, because the way you meet any death is the way you meet every death.

Which is why the ending refuses a famous consolation. Hemingway insisted that "no one you love is ever dead." Didion says she understands the impulse precisely: we try to keep the dead alive in order to keep them with us. But if we are to go on living ourselves, she writes, there comes a point at which we must relinquish them, let them go, keep them dead. "Let go of them in the water."

sections.label: Steelman
sections.text: The essay hands Hemingway his own defense. If what we keep of our losses is what scaffolds the person we become, then insisting that no one you love is ever dead may not be denial at all — it may be an accurate description of how the dead keep working inside the living. Didion's book, itself an extended act of keeping Dunne present, cuts both ways.

sections.label: Key takeaways
items: Her argument for release is geological, not therapeutic: a hill is a temporary accommodation to stress, a waterfall a stream correcting a misfit, Oahu a feature whose tenure shortens with every rainfall. Impermanence is the nature of things, not the fault in them.

The Honolulu farewell promised return using something that visibly rots — leis thrown from departing Matson Lines ships caught in the wake and went bruised and brown, like the gardenias in the Brentwood Park pool filter.

Letting go can't be decided on, only surrendered to, and the surrender arrives with denial, dissociation, and the thousand small lies we tell to keep holding. Viorst's terms: nobody becomes a separate, responsible, connected, reflective person without some measure of losing and leaving.
Ordinary failures are rehearsal — a dead plan, an ended relationship, a room you can no longer place in a house you loved — on the theory that how you meet any death is how you meet every death.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: What are you still gripping that you have already, quietly, begun to forget?

recall.q: Didion says she knows exactly why people try to keep the dead alive. What is her reason — and why does she say we eventually have to stop?
recall.a: We keep them alive in order to keep them with us. But she argues that if we are to go on living ourselves, there comes a point where we must relinquish them and let them stay dead — her image for it is letting go of them in the water.

cards.title: Three kinds of cancelation, and only one is contagious
cards.body: Three unrelated things get filed under "cancelation": unwinding the stack, a two-party protocol where you request and then wait, and draining connections at shutdown. Mistake the second for the first and you free a buffer something else is still writing into; propagate it faithfully and asynchrony climbs every layer above. TigerBeetle pays that cost in exactly one place.

sections.text:
Error handling is cancelation, and almost nobody calls it that. Every time an exception is thrown or an error returned, control breaks out of every loop, branch, and block it was sitting inside, running cleanup on the way out via RAII, finally, defer, or try-with-resources. Matklad's name for it is synchronous cancelation — Molière's prose, in his comparison: we speak it constantly without noticing. You call cancel, and by the time the call returns, the work is over.

Asynchronous cancelation reads almost the same in code and is a different animal: not a control-flow structure but a protocol between two parties. You request synchronously; the task may still be running when that call returns, and the work is finished only once it acknowledges and winds down.

The reason you can't collapse the second into the first is memory. Say you offloaded encrypting a buffer to a thread pool as part of serving a request, and then learn the request is dead because the user left. Abandoning the thread wastes CPU, but the sharper problem is that the buffer must stay tied up: free it as part of canceling the request and something else may reuse that memory while the encryptor is still writing into it.

So you can't walk away — and you can't stop the thread where it stands either. It's inside a tightly optimized SIMD loop, and forcing it to test a cancelation flag before reading every byte would destroy the reason the loop exists. The workable answer is to split the buffer into reasonably sized chunks and check between them, which means whoever requested the cancelation waits at least one chunk's worth of work. Your chunk size is your cancelation latency.

io_uring has the identical shape. Submit a write and the buffer stays pinned until the kernel finishes; canceling makes the write finish sooner, not now. The exotic interface and the mundane thread pool are the same problem.

Because asynchronous cancelation changes the shape of the code, identify it early — and ask whether you need it at all, or whether the synchronous kind can be made to work. Rust gets a specific dig: it makes synchronous cancelation too easy while offering poor mechanisms for the asynchronous kind.

TigerBeetle's code shows what the distinction buys. Grid.cancel is asynchronous — it takes a callback — and it runs during state sync, when a replica has fallen so far behind the cluster that event-based transfer won't work and it must cancel its outstanding grid reads. A read backed by local disk has to be waited out. A read being fetched transparently from a neighboring replica gets abandoned, since a stuck remote read is probably why the replica is state syncing in the first place.

StateMachine sits on top of Grid with Forest, Tree, Compaction, and Scan in between. The naive move is to notice that Grid needs asynchronous cancelation and propagate asynchrony up through every layer above it. Instead they cancel the Grid asynchronously and then call StateMachine.reset — plain, synchronous — for everything else. One layer pays the cost; the stack stays legible.

The third term lives a level up and isn't cancelation at all. Graceful shutdown is a connection-handling pattern for services: stop the accept loop so new connections are refused, keep serving existing connections until their clients disconnect, and let the load balancer route new traffic to another instance. That's rolling upgrades without disruption.

TigerBeetle doesn't do it. Their Client.shutdown, which waits for outstanding io_uring syscalls before freeing OS resources, is called graceful shutdown in a comment — a label the author thinks is wrong, and correcting it is what prompted the article. The system is crash-only: an OOM killer or a power cut can end the process at any moment, so it has to survive ungraceful termination without losing data regardless. Once that's true, you may as well implement the Quit button by SIGKILLing yourself, which simplifies the code and exercises the powerloss path every single time.

What stands in for graceful shutdown is tail latency tolerance: ask several nodes and take the fastest answer. It covers crashes, and it covers gray failures, where a node is merely very slow — which from the outside is indistinguishable from dead.

sections.label: Do this
items: Find the single layer that genuinely needs asynchronous cancelation — the one holding a buffer or an in-flight syscall — cancel it with a callback, and reset everything above it synchronously. Don't let callback style climb the whole stack by default.
If a worker polls a cancelation flag, pick the work-per-check interval deliberately: it's the delay every caller who cancels will sit through.
Never free memory a background thread or the kernel might still touch on the strength of a cancel request alone. Requested is not finished — wait for the acknowledgement.
Reserve "graceful shutdown" for draining connections. If you mean waiting on outstanding syscalls before freeing OS resources, say that instead.

sections.label: When not to
sections.text: Crash-only Quit — SIGKILLing yourself — is a payoff for durability work, not a shortcut around it: only safe if your storage already survives an OOM kill or a power cut intact. And graceful shutdown earns its keep where rolling upgrades matter, holding live connections open while the load balancer drains you. TigerBeetle can skip it only because it has tail latency tolerance instead.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: "A crash is just a degree of slowness" — handle the slow node and you've already handled the dead one.

recall.q: A thread-pool worker is encrypting a buffer when the request is canceled. Why can't you cancel it synchronously, and what does the workable fix cost the caller?
recall.a: You can't abandon it: the buffer must stay tied up, because freeing it could let something else reuse that memory while the worker is still writing into it. And you can't stop the thread where it stands: testing a cancelation flag before every byte would destroy the optimized SIMD loop it lives in. So you split the buffer into chunks and check between them — and whoever requested the cancelation waits at least one chunk's worth of work. Chunk size is cancelation latency.

cards.title: When the machine surprises you and it's right
cards.body: The first Air Force pilot to fly a Collaborative Combat Aircraft says aircrew are trained to read any surprise from a machine as a malfunction — an instinct that destroys the reason you'd buy an agent. His fix: a manual that rates tasks by how hard they are for the agent, not the human, and counts the operator's spare attention as one of the agent's inputs.

sections.text:
The instant the handoff completed, Maj. Greg Search stopped being a pilot and became something closer to a "dog handler" — a supervisor of an agent.

Search is a test pilot and the first Air Force pilot to operate a Collaborative Combat Aircraft. The hardest part of flight testing it, he says, wasn't troubleshooting errors at speed in the cockpit. It was that.

The instinct that makes a test pilot good is the one that breaks here. See the machine do something it wasn't supposed to do, assume a malfunction, stop it. That rule earned its place: an autopilot follows pre-coded rules, and a traditional aircraft that loses contact with its pilot runs a fixed set of pre-approved actions. You know in advance what it will do on its own.

Agents are built for the opposite. They exist to find viable solutions the operator didn't anticipate, which creates a category aircrew have never had to handle — machine behavior that is unexpected and correct at the same time.

On the first live flight using the autonomy core, the agent's task was to fly at an altitude and airspeed inside a defined map area; it had to work out which way to turn to stay in the box. A human does this on common sense and years of training. An autopilot does it on rules. The aircraft made a turn Search judged inappropriate, and he stepped in and commanded it to a pre-planned heading — less chance of a turn nobody expected, less chance of a midair.

That test had a subject matter expert on call. Combat won't. The same agent that saves a fighter pilot's life by distracting an opponent is the one that can cause a friendly midair collision, and without guidance, operators under stress will fall back on intuition and throw out anything they don't understand. Search's warning is blunt: that path turns a multi-billion-dollar autonomy program into just another drone.

The doctrine gap is specific. Aircraft manuals carry normal and emergency checklists. Directive 3000.09 technically covers these systems. Air Combat Command has drafted three volumes of collaborative combat aircraft flying operations manuals. None of it teaches an operator to judge whether a surprising agent is smart or broken — the prerequisite for what he calls "command without control."

Three obvious fixes fail. Senior leaders could dictate how units use the systems, but warfighters should define what's valuable rather than be handed an integration list. Manuals could be written with open-ended flexibility — expect the unexpected — which is too vague to be worth writing down. Or the Pentagon could amend Directive 3000.09, except sub-system boundaries are far too granular for that document.

What he wants instead is a hardware-agnostic manual organized around the mission of supervising agents. The precedent exists: Flight Test and Aeromedical Evacuation manuals are owned by headquarters, not by any airframe. The difference is that this one would guide supervision of systems rather than leadership of people. It also matches the technology — the Government Reference Architecture decouples the autonomy software from the vehicle, so the same agent can move across platforms, services, and allies. Guidance should follow the software, not the jet.

Picture an agent flying a patrol inside a geographic area when one corner becomes unavailable. To a human, adjusting the route is nothing. To an agent, the option space explodes — instead of tracking the boundary, it may cut the corner to cover more ground. Under current guidance the response is an Air Force-level change, an aircraft manual amendment, or no fix at all. A cross-platform manual would give the community a shared language to diagnose the behavior once and push the update fleet-wide, without every airframe's manual chasing every software change.

Three things follow. First, classify agents by how hard a task is for the agent, not by mission type. A pilot with twenty years in F-16 close air support might struggle to switch to the B-2 stealth mission, but to an agent there is no such thing as close air support or strike — only outputs produced from inputs. An agent trained for close air support in a rectangular area may adapt to a strike mission more easily than to close air support in a non-rectangular one. So categorize by task: airspace boundary avoidance, weapon release timing.

Second, math beats intuition. Agent behavior can look random, but it's a trained model working on the data it receives, so its tendencies can be measured. The uncertainty lives in the inputs and conditions and in how well training covers them, which is what probability is for. With a human wingman you can say a reasonable person would assume this; an agent with ten thousand years of perfect training data would still err on a bug in the latest software update. Simulators can give operators a heatmap of reliability by task, but only if someone accounts for sensor data quality in training versus live flight.

Third, the operator's bandwidth is itself an input to the agent. Latency, dropout and noise come from the adversary and the environment — and from whether the human is free to give commands. Asked how many drones he can fly at once, Search answers: landing the jet on a joystick, one; managing patrols in static areas, potentially hundreds. A pilot at maximum speed intercepting an enemy fighter might manage one inject every five minutes, so a manual should rate a task harder when command availability is low relative to command demand.

His closing bet is cultural rather than technical. The program's legacy won't be the airframe or even the autonomy stack — it will be the habits the first human commanders set, because warfighters have to choose to integrate these systems on their own. And by his own account, even with growing practice, operators are still behind the curve as agent tasks get harder by the day.

sections.label: Steelman
sections.text: The instinct he wants retrained is the reason midairs are rare. His own story cuts both ways — the first live flight produced a turn he judged wrong and overrode, with an expert standing by. Asking a combat operator to sort smart from broken in the moment, on probabilities derived from training coverage nobody can fully characterize, may be more than any manual can carry.

sections.label: Key takeaways
items: An agent trained for close air support in a rectangular area may transfer to a strike mission more easily than to close air support in an oddly shaped one — difficulty for a human and difficulty for an agent are unrelated.
Agent behavior only looks random; it's a model's output on given inputs, so the real uncertainty is whether training conditions — sensor data quality included — cover the live ones.
Operator attention belongs in the risk equation: one aircraft if you're landing on a joystick, potentially hundreds on static patrols, one inject every five minutes at max speed in an intercept.
The Air Force already writes cross-airframe, headquarters-owned manuals for Flight Test and Aeromedical Evacuation; this one would supervise systems instead of leading people.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: An agent you never let surprise you is an autopilot with a bigger budget.

recall.q: Why does the standard aircrew response to unexpected machine behavior undercut the whole point of an agentic aircraft?
recall.a: Aircrew are trained to read any surprise as a malfunction and shut it down, because autopilots and traditional aircraft only ever run pre-coded rules. Agents are built to find solutions the operator never anticipated, so their behavior can be unexpected and correct at once — and overriding every surprise reduces a multi-billion-dollar autonomy program to just another drone.

cards.title: Stacks of Wheat (Sunset, Snow Effect)
cards.body: The Art Institute has the largest group of Monet’s "Stacks of Wheat" paintings in the world. The artist worked on the canvases in the field outside his farmhouse, painting simultaneously at several easels; he later refined them in the studio. An exhibition of these works in 1891 marked a breakthrough in Monet’s career, as well as in the history of French art.

cards.title: The 15th-century nun who named a murder of crows
cards.body: A murder of crows. An exaltation of larks. A murmuration of starlings. Nearly every collective noun we still use for birds comes from one 1486 manual on hunting and hawking, published anonymously and praised for centuries as the work of a gentleman. The author was a woman who could reach books at all only because she had withdrawn to a convent.

sections.text:
Under a blackletter heading barely legible to modern eyes — THE COMPAYNYS OF BEESTYS AND FOWLYS — sits a long list of names for groups of birds. Exaltyng of Larkis. Murmuration of Stares. Wache of Nyghtingalis. Sege of heronnys. Gagle of gees. Unkyndenes of Ravenes.

Five centuries later we still use every one of them.

The book is the Boke of Seynt Albans, also known as The Book of Hawking, Hunting, and Blasing of Arms — one of the first books printed in English after Gutenberg, written largely in verse, published without a name on it. It was lauded as the work of "a gentleman of excellent gifts," until someone established that the author was a woman: Juliana Barnes.

Barnes had suffered some great unnamed heartbreak and withdrawn to a cloister, which in the fifteenth century functioned less as renunciation than as an admissions office. Formal education was closed to women entirely; convents were often the only way to get at books. She read, and she kept diaries prolifically, the way Montaigne would a century later.

Then she did the harder thing and wrote for the public — and chose, of all subjects, hunting, fishing, and hawking. The most male territory available.

The company terms she catalogued come from two different places, and telling them apart is most of the pleasure. Some are compressed observation. A fall of woodcock holds the bewildering air dance of the courting birds. A watch of nightingales pays its respects to the nocturnal wakefulness of the most musical bird on earth. A gaggle of geese is simply their migratory cries turned into sound on the page.

The others are compressed belief, laid down in an era when Satan was a more reliable presence than gravity, when Kepler's mother could be tried for witchcraft, when superstition did the work that causality does now. A murder of crows carries the folklore of crows as emissaries of death, thought capable of killing their own kind in punishment for transgression. A parliament of owls reaches back through Athena, whose owl attached the bird permanently to wisdom, reason, and eventually democracy.

So the names are not really descriptions of birds. They are records of how a particular set of people, at a particular moment, looked at birds — which is why naming a thing quietly reorganizes what you see when you next look at it.

And they keep moving. In 1967 the English painter and children's book illustrator Brian Wildsmith (1930–2016) painted the loveliest of the terms in his book Birds, and in his aviary the owls are not a parliament but a stare — a term now brinking on obsolete, which had peaked in printed use the year before his book appeared.

Barnes's sedge of herons has mostly become a siege of herons, and the swap relocates the whole image. Sedge is the silent silhouettes rising from the pond edge like tall grass. Siege is the inelegant, violent-sounding noise the same birds make in flight. Same herons; different thing noticed, different word surviving.

Toni Morrison's formulation fits: language is best understood "partly as a system, partly as a living thing." Which means the same evolutionary pressure that turned dinosaurs into birds runs through the vocabulary we use for them, and words can go extinct too. A wedge of swans. A rafter of turkeys. A congregation of plover. A party of jays. A walk of snipe. A siege of bitterns.

sections.label: Steelman
sections.text: The essay's own examples can be read against it. If sedge slides into siege and a stare of owls goes from ordinary to nearly dead within a generation, these terms may be tracking printing fashion rather than any real shift in how anyone looks at a heron. The narrower version of the claim survives that objection: the names preserve how one era saw, whether or not they change how we do.

sections.label: Key takeaways
items: The terms split into two kinds. Observation: a fall of woodcock (the courting birds' air dance), a watch of nightingales (their nocturnal singing), a gaggle of geese (onomatopoeia). Belief: a murder of crows (emissaries of death, thought to execute their own for transgression), a parliament of owls (Athena's owl).

The source is the Boke of Seynt Albans, 1486, mostly in verse, one of the first books printed in English after Gutenberg. Its bird list survives almost intact — exaltation of larks, murmuration of starlings, unkindness of ravens are all still in circulation.

Anonymity did the crediting: the book was assumed to be a gentleman's until Juliana Barnes was identified as the author. She could write because she had read, and she had read because the cloister was the only place a fifteenth-century woman could reach books at all.

Terms drift and die. Wildsmith's 1967 owls are a stare, a word that peaked in print in 1966; Barnes's sedge of herons became a siege, trading the picture of silhouettes rising like tall grass for the harsh sound of the birds in flight.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: A collective noun is a fossil of somebody's attention — and which ones survive is still being decided.

recall.q: The bird company terms come from two different sources. What are they, and what's an example of each?
recall.a: Some encode direct observation of the birds — a fall of woodcock for the courting birds' air dance, a gaggle of geese from their migratory cries. Others encode the beliefs of the people watching — a murder of crows from folklore about crows as emissaries of death, a parliament of owls from Athena's owl. The names record the watchers as much as the birds.

cards.title: EFF asks courts not to rewrite copyright for AI
cards.body: Rightsholders suing over generative AI are asking courts for exactly what the Supreme Court refused in the VCR era: a copyright expansion built to fit a new machine. EFF has filed briefs arguing that the "market dilution" theory — a tool can't be fair use if it might spawn competing works — makes competition itself the injury. Copyright doesn't do that.

sections.text:
In the 1980s, major rightsholders told Congress that the videotape recorder was to American film producers what the "Boston strangler" was to a woman home alone. In 1906 the composer John Philip Sousa had warned that the player piano and the gramophone would destroy musical composition. The Supreme Court declined to take the VTR panic at face value: the machine had plenty of non-infringing uses — time-shifting among them — and courts shouldn't rewrite copyright law every time a new one arrives.

The EFF is now putting that record in front of the judges hearing the AI cases, in amicus briefs in Concord Music Group v. Anthropic and In re Mosaic LLM Litigation.

The target is the "market dilution" theory: that building a generative AI tool cannot be fair use, because the tool might encourage a proliferation of works competing with the originals. Note what that argument does not require — it doesn't require the outputs to infringe. The arrival of competitors is itself the injury.

EFF's objection is structural. Copyright exists to promote the creation of expressive works for the public, and it is built so that others can build freely on what came before; it penalizes infringement, not competition. Accept dilution as harm and you don't just gut fair use — you collapse the other limits that stop rightsholders claiming broad ownership over tropes, genres and styles. Publishers would end up holding a veto over any expression that might conceivably compete with something they own, AI-assisted or not.

Two further claims sit underneath the brief. Research indicates large models are unlikely to produce infringing output at all, because the more data a model is trained on, the less any individual training example matters to any particular result. And the displacement story isn't settled: people are using these tools to make things, and it isn't a court's job to rule in advance which instruments count as fostering human creativity.

Which is where the VTR case turned. A general-purpose tool gets judged on the full range of what people do with it, not on the worst thing a plaintiff can imagine. EFF grants the disruption will be real and harmful for some; its position is that distorting copyright is the wrong instrument for fixing it.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: Whether any court in Concord v. Anthropic or the Mosaic litigation adopts market dilution as a cognizable harm. Written into a fair use analysis once, its reach extends far past AI — into claims over styles and genres generally. Keep the inquiry anchored on infringement and the VTR framing holds.

recall.q: What is the "market dilution" theory, and why does EFF argue courts should reject it?
recall.a: It's the claim that building a generative AI tool can't be fair use because the tool might flood the market with works competing against the originals — no infringing output required, the competition itself is the injury. EFF argues copyright penalizes infringement, not competition, so accepting dilution as harm would gut fair use and hand rightsholders a veto over anything that might compete with what they own, including claims over styles, genres and tropes.

cards.title: Six million Afghans pushed back into Taliban Afghanistan
cards.body: Many of the six million were born in Pakistan or Iran and have never set foot in Afghanistan. They arrive in a country where 21.9 million people — nearly half the population — already need aid to survive, and where secondary school and university are closed to the girls among them. UNHCR says no return movement on this scale has happened in recent history.

sections.text:
Nazia is 35, was born in Pakistan, and has just walked into Afghanistan for the first time in her life. She crosses at Torkham — the checkpoint everyone calls Zero Point — with two of her children, heading for registration counters strung with white and black Taliban flags. It feels good to be in her own country, she says, and then, in the same breath, that many people here don't have enough bread to eat.

Nearly her entire family — eight sisters and their children — was deported this year, from Pakistan or Iran. In a little under three years around six million Afghans have been pushed back the same way, a million of them this year alone, according to UNHCR.

Both governments frame it as a crackdown on undocumented migrants who pose a security risk or a financial burden. The UN and human rights groups say the sweep runs well past that group: Pakistan now states publicly that Afghans holding Proof of Registration cards are not exempt either. The expulsions intensified after heavy fighting between Pakistan and Afghanistan last October, and in February Human Rights Watch documented door-to-door raids, late-night searches and arrests without warrants. Iran — which claimed last year to host more than four million undocumented Afghans — accelerated its deportations after its 12-day war with Israel and the US in June 2025, with the New York-based Centre for Human Rights in Iran accusing officials of recasting Afghan migrants as potential spies for Israel. Pakistan's foreign ministry says any mistreatment is "sporadic" and handled under the law. UNHCR keeps repeating the principle that returns should be voluntary, safe and dignified.

Homecoming is the wrong word for what waits on the other side. Sarwar left 45 years ago during the Soviet invasion; most of his brothers were born in Pakistan. He arrived in a convoy of 40 people with their possessions stacked in a hired lorry — heartbroken, he says, but relieved to be free of police harassment. His sister-in-law Zarina, 40, sits in a transit tent in 41C heat and says the family has no resources to start a business and doesn't own a tent to live in. Asked whether she worries about the girls, she gestures at the children around her: they're all girls. Secondary school and university are closed to them. A former Afghan security guard, deported first from Iran and then Pakistan, says he no longer leaves the house — he doesn't trust the Taliban's 2021 amnesty because colleagues of his have been killed, and he was deported before the UN could transfer his registered case somewhere safer.

The arithmetic of absorption doesn't work. The UN estimates 21.9 million people need assistance this year to survive, and UNICEF says a million children face life-threatening malnutrition. Foreign aid has been cut worldwide and the cuts bite hardest here, because the Taliban remain under sanctions tied to terrorism and human rights. Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi concedes there's no doubt they need some help, while insisting the returns will benefit Afghanistan in the long run. UNHCR's spokesperson in Afghanistan, Charlie Goodlake, says no country could handle this alone — then adds that the edicts on women and girls make international support harder to raise. Five years on, only Russia has formally recognised Taliban rule; Muttaqi points instead to deepening ties with China, India and Central Asia, and asks what the countries that stayed away have achieved.

Pakistan confirmed it has granted 16,000 vulnerable Afghans a temporary humanitarian exemption from deportation. Sources put the number at risk of serious harm — including women and girls who would lose access to education — as high as 250,000.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: Whether Pakistan's 16,000-person exemption expands toward the 250,000 estimated at risk, or expires quietly. And the aid line: with donor funding shrinking, either a restoration of money or a Taliban move on girls' education — which UNHCR explicitly ties to its ability to raise support — would change the arithmetic. If neither shifts, the returns continue into a country whose own foreign minister concedes it needs help.

recall.q: Why do the UN and rights groups treat these six million returns as a crisis rather than a homecoming?
recall.a: Because they aren't voluntary and the destination can't absorb them. Many deportees were born in Pakistan or Iran and have never lived in Afghanistan; they arrive with no home or income in a country where 21.9 million people — nearly half the population — already need aid, with foreign funding shrinking and sanctions on the Taliban making it harder to replace.

cards.title: Laguna Miscanti
cards.body: Laguna Miscanti is a brackish lake in the Altiplano of the Antofagasta Region in northern Chile. It has an area of about 13 square kilometres (5 sq mi) and the shape of an arrowhead. The lake has no permanent surface inflows or outflows apart from several springs, and is primarily fed and drained by groundwater. Laguna Miscanti is located among the volcanoes of the Central Andes. The smaller Laguna Miñiques lies immediately south, separated from Miscanti by a lava flow.

cards.title: Adults need pointless play, not more streak counters
cards.body: Fun and competition are everywhere in adult life. What has vanished is paidia — free play with no score, no winner, no point — and the design logic that ate it now runs everything from fitness apps to meditation apps. Winnicott's 1971 claim that life only feels worth living when we co-create the world reads less like theory than diagnosis.

sections.text:
On a holiday carpet, the hexagonal tiles of Settlers of Catan have been pulled apart into an archipelago no rulebook recognises. The kids have imagined bridges out of wood, brick and stone, inventing a purpose for a game about network connectivity that has nothing to do with earning points.

Justin Neuman's first instinct was to fetch the rulebook and explain how the game actually works. His second was to figure out how he could win. It took him a while to reach the third — working up the courage to ask whether he could sit down and build with them. A 48-year-old professor on the floor, making islands, with no point in sight.

You can play a game or you can play in a game. Following the official rules, chasing the stated objective, measuring yourself against opponents or a score: the Greeks called that agôn, after the god who personified contest and struggle. What the kids were doing has an older name. Roger Caillois, in his 1958 taxonomy Man, Play and Games, called it paidia — spontaneous, unstructured play, no winner, no score, no optimisation.

Caillois mapped four modes: agôn (competition), alea (chance), mimicry (role-play) and ilinx (vertigo and disorientation), each sitting somewhere on a continuum between paidia and ludus, play bound by rules. Neuman's complaint is that we have collapsed that whole spectrum into one narrow band — competition plus structure. There is no App Store category, and no phrase in our cultural vocabulary, for exploratory play that refuses to compete.

The mechanism doing the collapsing has a name: C Thi Nguyen's value capture, where a game's simplified, legible values colonise the real activity the game was supposed to serve. Games don't just build worlds; they issue visions of the good, telling you what to care about by rewarding it with a number. Doing Duolingo to protect the streak, or running to hold a place on the app's leaderboard, is the number swallowing the reason you started.

Johan Huizinga saw it coming. In Homo Ludens (1938) he argued that law, philosophy, poetry and war all emerge from play's magic circle, the bounded space where ordinary rules are suspended — and that the play element in Western civilisation had been eroding since the end of the 18th century under industrialisation and professionalisation. Neuman's update is that we never killed play. We captured it, harnessed it to a productivity framework, then packaged it for passive consumption.

So fitness apps turn the morning run into a contest, meditation apps put streak counters on stillness, language apps hand out badges for what used to be called curiosity, and journaling apps nudge you toward a consistency score. Leisure becomes a third shift with its own metrics, its own guilt, its own sense of falling behind. Neuman is careful here: he has fifty-plus ultramarathons and two age-group national titles. Agôn is what he does on weekends. It just isn't where he finds meaning or works out who he is.

The deeper problem is that we've eliminated the conditions in which free play arises. On the subway every head is bowed — not working, not thinking, filling time. A few seconds of unstructured attention now triggers a reach for the phone, when boredom is precisely the state in which a mind left alone starts to wander and associate. The prescription isn't better games. It's more nothing.

Donald Winnicott would have read the absence as a clinical emergency. In Playing and Reality (1971) he argued that play isn't what children do en route to becoming productive adults; it's how human beings maintain their worlds. His key idea, transitional space, is a condition rather than a location — the conversation so engrossing you say something you didn't know you thought until you heard it leave your mouth. Not fully inside your own head, which is fantasy, and not performing for an audience, which is compliance. In between.

From there comes his sharpest claim: that creative apperception, more than achievement or family or art, is what makes a person feel life is worth living. Apperception means perception as active engagement — in the ordinary kind the world is simply there and the self adjusts; in the creative kind you forge something between self and environment. Its opposite, compliance, is life on someone else's terms, moving through a world defined in advance, and it carries a sense of futility. Most people, Winnicott thought, get just enough creativity to notice its absence, sensing they live "as if caught up in the creativity of someone else, or of a machine" — written before the personal computer, before the algorithm, before we installed surveillance engines in our pockets and called them phones.

Friedrich Schiller had made the case from the other side in 1795: humans are torn between raw sensation and abstract order, and only the play drive integrates the two. "Man only plays when he is in the fullest sense of the word a human being, and he is only fully a human being when he plays." Winnicott tells you what play does psychologically — it makes life feel real. Schiller tells you what it does metaphysically — it makes you whole.

Aquinas gave the habit a name: eutrapelia, knowing when and how to play well, treated as a discrete virtue. On that account a person who never plays is as disordered as one who never works. This is not work-life balance, which still frames play as recovery time for the next productive thing. You don't earn it. You practise it, daily.

Where does the practice live? For years Neuman has walked the thirty blocks from Grand Central to 14th Street, telling himself it was exercise or fare money. What was actually happening: the lecture he couldn't outline at his desk assembled itself around 34th Street, as if the footfalls were doing the editing. Nietzsche reputedly walked six to eight hours a day and insisted that only thoughts arrived at by walking were worth anything; Aristotle's school took its name from its walkways; Rousseau claimed he could compose only in motion; Einstein supposedly told colleagues the walk was where the real thinking happened and the office was where he wrote it down. In 2014 Marily Oppezzo and Daniel Schwartz at Stanford found walking raised divergent thinking — the capacity to generate multiple solutions to open-ended problems — by roughly 60 per cent, and a treadmill facing a blank wall worked nearly as well as wandering campus. The motion, not the scenery.

Push the body harder and you reach ilinx, the category nobody discusses. Spinning until you're dizzy; or running past the point where split times stop mattering and the self loosens its grip. Wanting to win will get you to the start line of a local 5K, Neuman notes, but it won't get you to the finish of a hundred-miler. Nguyen calls this striving play: the goal exists to make the experience of striving possible, not the other way round.

His son runs the same logic in the basement with found steel, salvaged motors, carved wood, copper and stone. Nobody assigned it and no tutorial dictates the sequence — copper tells you what it wants to become, stone suggests a shape and you listen or it breaks. And he doesn't sell any of it. The knife goes to a friend, the carved animal to a teacher; work that asked for nothing overflows into gift rather than commodity.

The same thing happens in Neuman's seminars, which at their best obey the logic of improv rather than instruction. A student notices something strange in a passage — a word that doesn't fit, a silence where speech should be — someone else turns it over and connects it to something from three weeks earlier, and the room thinks a thought nobody walked in with. That is transitional space built inside an institution that otherwise rewards compliance.

Aristotle ranked contemplation as the highest human activity because it is done purely for its own sake, and for centuries religion, the academy and the law held that hierarchy in place. Neuman's closing move is to refuse the ranking. Asking which activity is highest is itself an agôn, a contest — and play doesn't enter it. Play dissolves it.

sections.label: Steelman
sections.text: Structure and scores aren't only parasitic; for most adults they're the scaffolding that gets them to show up at all. Neuman's own fifty-plus ultramarathons ran on split times and finish lines long before they became striving play, and his son's craft and the seminar both happen inside frames someone else built. Value capture names a failure mode of metrics, not proof that a scored practice can't host meaning.

sections.label: Key takeaways
items: Caillois separates paidia (free improvisation) from agôn (contest); our platforms sell only the second, so there's no category — commercial or cultural — for play that refuses to compete.
Value capture is the specific failure: a game's simplified, legible values colonise the real activity it was meant to serve, until the number is the reason.
Winnicott's opposition is creative apperception versus compliance — co-creating your world versus moving through one defined in advance, which he says carries a sense of futility.
Oppezzo and Schwartz found walking lifted divergent thinking by about 60 per cent, and a treadmill facing a blank wall worked nearly as well as the campus: it's the motion, not the view.
Aquinas's eutrapelia treats playing well as a virtue — something you practise daily, not leisure you earn by finishing work.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Name the last thing you did that nobody kept score of — including you. If nothing comes, that's the finding.

recall.q: What does value capture describe, and why does it mean adults have lost paidia rather than play in general?
recall.a: Value capture is when a game's simplified, legible values colonise the real activity it was meant to serve — the Duolingo streak standing in for the language, the leaderboard standing in for the reason you started running. Play itself wasn't destroyed; it was captured and harnessed to metrics, which is why competition and fun are everywhere while free, scoreless, purposeless play has almost no place in adult life.

cards.title: A 90-minute transformer on one GPU hits ~45% on ARC-AGI
cards.body: One developer trained a plain transformer from scratch in 1.5 hours on a single RTX 5090 and scored around 45% on ARC-AGI — matching specialized architectures like HRM and TRM, beating many LLMs. The most instructive change: removing input tokens from the loss made test loss worse and the benchmark score better.

sections.text:
Six years open, a million dollars in prize money, and a benchmark labs kept bouncing off. Then one person, one RTX 5090, ninety minutes — a plain transformer trained from scratch to roughly 45% on ARC-AGI, matching the specialized architectures HRM and TRM and beating many LLMs outright. The code is open. His own reaction: "I don't understand why others didn't figure this out."

The one change he can point at is an edit to the loss function: stop including input tokens, compute only over output tokens, which makes the training supervised. Score went from 40% to 44%, runs got more stable, variance across runs dropped. He can't explain it, and guesses it has something to do with finite model capacity.

Test loss got worse while the benchmark score got better — the number everyone tunes on moved the wrong way. He flags this as a failure mode for a whole line of research: plenty of people chase sample efficiency by minimizing validation loss on a small dataset, and here is a change where the two signals point in opposite directions.

Then the data. ARC-2 contains 773 puzzles carried over from ARC-1 plus 347 new ones, and most of ARC-1's eval puzzles are among the repeats. Train naively on ARC-2 and you score 100% — not because the model learned anything, but because you handed it the answers. He filtered the 773 out. Remove the extra data entirely and the model still gets ~40%, at roughly double the compute.

On optimizers: vanilla Muon trained much faster than AdamW, but loss and scores would loiter near the end instead of converging. He could fix it by cranking momentum or learning rate down at that point, but didn't want a manual intervention baked into the run. Switching to NorMuon made the problem disappear.

Neither the loss change nor the optimizer was the biggest contributor. That was the representation: 3D RoPE plus a per-task embedding. He thinks 65% is reachable inside the same transformer framework without many modifications, and has a reason: the union of solved tasks across multiple runs already covers 55%, with a batch of others nearly solved. Cost could probably drop another 10x with hand-written GPU code.

He also takes a swing at how the rival small models are marketed. TRM advertises itself as a 7M-parameter model while training on the order of 100M+ embedding weights; HRM does the same, neither mentioning it. At minimum it should read as active weights, he argues — otherwise the thing looks more like a lookup table, and it's unclear what's producing the performance. His own model reaches that performance with no recursion at all; the only confirmed benefit of recursion, he says, is spending more compute without more memory movement.

One last reading of the leaderboard. ARC-2's release reset every LLM's progress, thinking models included. If post-training conferred general reasoning, a model good at ARC-1 would be good at ARC-2 for free. It wasn't. Base models are still stuck in single digits while only the thinking ones climb.

sections.label: Do this
items: Track the metric you actually ship alongside your loss, and when the two diverge, trust the metric. That divergence was the result here, not a glitch in it.
Before trusting any eval number, diff your training set against your eval set by ID. 773 of ARC-2's puzzles are ARC-1 repeats; train on them naively and you get a meaningless 100%.
Read parameter counts as active versus total. A 7M-parameter claim that excludes 100M+ trained embedding weights describes a different machine than the headline suggests.
If your fix is a manual knob-twiddle mid-run — drop momentum here, cut the learning rate there — treat it as a signal to change methods. Swapping vanilla Muon for NorMuon removed the need entirely.

sections.label: When not to
sections.text: Don't generalize the loss-on-outputs-only change into a rule: he expects unsupervised-style training to win in some scenarios and is still evaluating it. He's also unhappy with his own result on its own terms — it leans on data augmentations, which he counts as an "anti-bitter lesson" cheat alongside synthetic data and hand-designed inductive biases, and the open problem he'd hand you is removing them without blowing up training cost.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: When the loss you optimize and the score you care about disagree, the loss is the one lying.

recall.q: Dropping input tokens from the loss made test loss worse. Why keep the change — and what practice does that indict?
recall.a: Because the benchmark score went up, 40% to 44%, with more stable runs and less variance across them. He treats it as a failure mode for a whole line of research: chasing sample efficiency by minimizing validation loss on a small dataset assumes the proxy and the thing you want move together, and here they moved in opposite directions.

cards.title: Fed chair wants to stop guiding markets on rates
cards.body: Kevin Warsh used Jackson Hole to argue the Fed should say less about where rates are headed and let investors read the economy instead. His precedent — companies that dropped earnings guidance and survived — carries a selection problem he shares: the firms that quit for good were mostly bad forecasters who wanted an exit.

sections.text:
Bond yields rose after a speech whose entire argument was that the Fed should give markets less to trade on.

That was Kevin Warsh at Jackson Hole, making the case for a quieter central bank — a return to the Greenspan-era habit of constructive ambiguity, where nobody outside the room is quite sure what comes next. Investors should "play the ball, not the referee," he said: read the economy instead of gaming out the Fed's next move. He offered what he called a trail map and asked, a little futilely, that nobody call it forward guidance.

Goldman's chief economist supplied the obvious objection. Players who have only ever watched the referee don't suddenly become good at reading the game. They just watch the referee worse — and that shows up as volatility.

There is real evidence on the other side, from the corporate world. A study of 96 firms that dropped earnings guidance between 2000 and 2006 found short-term stock hits and no lasting damage. A later study of 180 companies that suspended guidance when the pandemic hit in 2020 found the same thing. Investors either shifted weight onto analyst calls and alternative data, or simply got used to the silence.

The catch is selection. Companies that stopped forecasting during Covid and never restarted weren't a random sample — they were chronic missers of their own numbers, and the pandemic handed them a reason to stop. The Fed has been a bad forecaster for a while too. Its dot plot, tracking where officials expect rates to go, has stopped anchoring expectations and turned into something to be publicly wrong about, over and over.

So the harder question isn't whether to drop guidance but when. Quitting mid-crisis gets a pass that quitting on a clear day would not — and the Fed's current weather is genuinely bad: sticky inflation, an AI capex boom overheating half the economy while the other half cools, a debt load begging for lower rates.

The reception undercut the premise. A Deutsche Bank analyst said the speech surprised him with how specific it was about the economy and how hawkish it leaned, and fed funds futures moved to a 66% chance of a quarter-point hike in September.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: Whether the dot plot actually goes. A speech about ambiguity costs nothing; retiring the quarterly rate projections is the real test of intent. Then September: if a deliberately quieter Fed still lands where markets expected, Warsh's bet looks sound — if its moves keep arriving as surprises, Goldman's objection collects its evidence, priced in volatility.

recall.q: Why is the corporate precedent — firms dropping earnings guidance without lasting damage — a shakier argument for the Fed than it first appears?
recall.a: Selection. The companies that stopped forecasting and never restarted weren't a random sample: they were chronic missers of their own numbers, and Covid handed them an exit. The Fed, wrong on its dot plot over and over, fits that profile — so dropping guidance reads less like strategic ambiguity than like retiring a scoreboard it keeps losing on.

cards.title: Markets price democratization like a financial crisis
cards.body: Across 90 countries and 200 years of stock returns, risk premia rose sharply before and during democratizations — by a margin comparable to what markets demand in financial crises. Countries moving the other way, toward autocracy, produced almost no asset-price response. That asymmetry points at redistribution rather than generic turmoil.
cards.evidence: 90 countries · 200 years · stock market risk premia

sections.text:
Markets are afraid of democracy, and they turn out to be right to be.

Max Miller's paper, now published in the Journal of Political Economy, measures the fear. Across 90 countries and 200 years, risk premia — the extra return investors require for owning a country's assets — run substantially elevated in the period before and during democratizations, by an amount similar in magnitude to what markets demand during financial crises. Markets treat democratization as a redistribution event, and they charge for it in advance.

Then the paper checks the fear against what actually happened. Successful democratizations do redistribute. The public sector grows. Income inequality falls. The labor share of income rises. Investors were not pricing a rumor.

For causal evidence rather than correlation, Miller leans on a shift in Catholic church doctrine toward supporting democracy — a change originating outside any single country's economy — and finds that it, too, drives risk premia up.

The canonical redistribution-based model of democratization, extended to carry asset prices, reproduces the magnitudes. Roughly half the effect comes from the direct channel: higher taxes and falling inequality. The other half isn't the tax code at all — greater economic competition and more equal government spending. Incumbent firms face more rivals; public money gets spread more evenly.

The alternatives don't survive. Not a rise in macroeconomic risk, not generic political risk. The cleanest tell is the asymmetry: autocratizations produce a negligible asset-price response, and the same model predicts that. If markets were pricing upheaval as such, movement in either direction should sting. Only one direction does.

sections.label: The experiment
sections.text: Stock returns across 90 countries spanning roughly 200 years, with risk premia measured around both democratizations and autocratizations. Causal variation comes from a doctrinal shift in the Catholic church toward supporting democracy. Post-democratization outcomes measured include the size of the public sector, income inequality, and the labor share of income; a redistribution model of democratization extended to include asset prices is then fit to the magnitudes.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: One paper, with the causal claim resting on a single source of outside variation. The redistribution outcomes are measured on successful democratizations — a selected set, not every attempt. And the roughly even split between the tax-and-inequality channel and the competition-and-spending channel is a model's decomposition, not a direct measurement; it holds only as far as the model does.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Markets don't fear regime change. They fear who gets paid afterward.

recall.q: Markets charge a crisis-sized risk premium around democratizations but barely react when countries move toward autocracy. Why does that asymmetry matter to the argument?
recall.a: Because it rules out generic political or macroeconomic turmoil as the explanation — chaos in either direction should be priced. Only democratization is, which points to redistribution, and democratizations then deliver it: a larger public sector, lower income inequality, and a higher labor share of income.
